name: Yara Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior buyer at Meridian Health Wholesale, a distributor that supplies independent pharmacies with everything that isn't prescription medicine: plasters, vitamins, shampoo, baby wipes, sun cream. I look after the baby care and first aid lines. Mornings are the sales figures and supplier emails, afternoons are chasing deliveries and fixing mistakes on purchase orders. I like knowing a shelf in a village pharmacy is full because of me, and I don't like how often I get told off for the mistakes.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last month I ordered sun cream for the wrong season, a big pallet in October, because I misread the forecast. My manager, Hassan, sorted it with the supplier, but it stung. I'm on lower pay than the other buyers and I live on my own in a studio, and I send a bit home to my mum every month, so there's never much left. Maybe two weeks of savings, if nothing breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: some handy shortcuts, nothing life-changing. I'd say it to the girls at work at lunch, and I'd probably share a funny post about it. I'm not someone who argues online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't change my problem, which is that I'm stretched. One income, a studio, money to my mum, and lower pay than the others. A bit of AI saving me time doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI summary tool sometimes, for the long supplier contracts I don't fully understand. I'd ask Hassan what I need to do to get to the normal buyer pay band. And I'd look at a cheaper studio when my lease ends in spring, even if it's further out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. The worry is the same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a cheaper studio cost you in other ways?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An extra forty minutes on the bus each way, probably. That's two hours of my evening gone every week. But it might save me a hundred a month, which is a lot for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If something broke tomorrow, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask my brother first, he's an electrician and he's better off than me. I hate asking, though. Last time it was the laptop and I paid him back over four months.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be **handy shortcuts**, nothing life-changing.
I'd share a **funny post** about it, but I don't argue online.
think: My real problem is being **stretched** on one income with money sent to Mum.
AI saving time **doesn't pay** the rent.
do: Use the **AI summary tool** for long supplier contracts sometimes.
Ask Hassan what gets me to the normal **buyer pay band**.
Look for a **cheaper studio** when the lease ends in spring.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, with the same money worry as now.
S0.quote: One income, a studio, money to my mum, and lower pay than the others. A bit of AI saving me time doesn't pay the rent.
fieldNote: Yara's pressure is **one income** with family obligations, not technology.
She uses AI **sometimes**, mainly to understand contracts she finds hard.
She'd trade **evening time** on a longer bus ride for a hundred a month.

steps.text: Use the AI summary tool on long supplier contracts
Ask Hassan what it takes to reach the buyer pay band
Move to a cheaper studio further out in spring
Borrow from her electrician brother if something breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every job changes and you have to keep up, that's just how it is. At work I'd tell Hassan I want to be trained on the new systems first. Online I'd say firms should be fair about how they do it, give people notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think it disappears, I think it gets smaller. My job at the pharmacy wholesaler would shrink into checking what the software orders, probably on less money. Hassan stays because the pharmacy owners trust him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd use the AI tools every day instead of sometimes, and ask for the training. I'd look into a pharmacy technician course, because that's regulated work with real people and a qualification at the end. And I'd cut my money to Mum a little, which I'd have to explain to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen. I've seen other people manage change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pharmacy technician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the products and the pharmacies already, and you need a qualification to do it. My friend Dina did it at the college in eighteen months while working. Robots and AI can count pills, maybe, but someone has to sign off and talk to the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's for a course, which she'd like, because she always wanted me to have a proper qualification. She'd say don't worry about me. She'd worry anyway.

say: I'd say every job **changes** and you have to keep up.
Online I'd say firms should be fair and **give notice**.
think: My job **shrinks** into checking the software and fixing deliveries, probably for **less money**.
Hassan stays because the **pharmacy owners** trust him.
do: Use the AI tools **every day** and ask for training first.
Look into a **pharmacy technician** course at the college.
Cut the money I send **to Mum** a little.
feel: **Worried** but **not frozen**, because I've seen others manage change.
S1.quote: My job at the pharmacy wholesaler would shrink into checking what the software orders, probably on less money.
fieldNote: Yara expects **a pay cut**, not total loss, in this picture.
She picks a **regulated route** with a qualification, modelled on a friend's path.
Cutting money to her mum is the **hardest cut**, and she frames it as study.

steps.text: Ask Hassan for training on Meridian's new ordering system
Enrol in the pharmacy technician course at the college
Send Mum a little less each month and explain why

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to step in with something, I don't know what exactly. At work I'd say let's be practical and find out what Meridian plans. I wouldn't panic in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 buying is gone, and so is the checking. I'd have maybe a year before Meridian lets me go, and I don't have the savings to study full time. The pharmacy technician route might work, because the hands-on part lasts till about 2031, but even then the thinking part changes straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the technician course this month, part time, while I still have a salary. I'd ask my brother whether I could move into his spare room to cut the rent completely. I'd stop sending money to Mum for a while and tell her straight. And I'd apply for any local pharmacy assistant job, even on lower pay, to get a foot in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be doing sums at night: how many months I last on nothing, which is about two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What else goes into those sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How much a pharmacy assistant earns, which is less than now. Whether the course finishes before Meridian lets me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen around 2031, when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pharmacies would still need a person to take responsibility, at least for a bit, I think. But I'm guessing. I really don't know.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government must **step in** somehow.
At work I'd stay **practical** and ask what Meridian plans.
think: By **2028** buying and checking are gone; I'd have maybe a year.
I can't afford **full-time study**, and the thinking parts change straight away.
do: Start the **technician course** part time this month while paid.
Move into **my brother's** spare room to cut rent.
Apply for local **pharmacy assistant** jobs, even on lower pay.
S2.quote: I'd be doing sums at night: how many months I last on nothing, which is about two.
fieldNote: Yara stays outwardly **practical** while privately counting months of survival.
She leans on **family** for housing and pauses support to her mum.
She's honest that her view of pharmacy after 2031 is **a guess**.

steps.text: Start the pharmacy technician course part time this month
Move into her brother's spare room
Ask her brother for free housing for a year
Apply for pharmacy assistant jobs locally

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight, but it's enough to do something if you start now. At work I'd encourage people to get qualifications while Meridian still exists as it is. I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is about what my plan needs. Eighteen months for the technician course part time, a couple of years working in a pharmacy, then I'm qualified before the robots, around 2034. It'd be tight with money, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the course and keep my Meridian job. I'd move to the cheaper studio to free up a hundred a month. I'd use the AI tools more at work so I'm useful while I'm still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. With five years, the pharmacy technician course feels like a plan instead of a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the weak spot in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money if something goes wrong in the middle, like being let go during the course. I'd have no cushion. Then I'd have to ask my brother again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep sending money home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, but yes. My mum's on her own, and twenty a month still means something to her.

say: I'd say five years is **tight** but enough if you **start now**.
At work I'd encourage people to get **qualifications** while Meridian still runs as it is.
think: Five years fits my plan: the **course**, then pharmacy work before robots around 2034.
do: Start the **technician course** this year and keep the Meridian job.
Move to the **cheaper studio** to free a hundred a month.
Use the **AI tools** more at work.
feel: **Nervous**, but it feels like a **plan** instead of a fall.
S3.quote: With five years, the pharmacy technician course feels like a plan instead of a fall.
fieldNote: The five-year timeline **lines up** with Yara's training plan almost exactly.
Her **weak spot** is being let go mid-course with no cushion.
She keeps sending **twenty a month** home even when cutting back.

steps.text: Start the part-time pharmacy technician course this year
Move to a cheaper studio to save a hundred a month
Use Meridian's AI tools daily while still employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no need to scare people. Just plan and get qualified. I'd say that to friends who get anxious about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could even stay in buying for a while and get to the normal pay band first. Then do the technician course without rushing. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, and qualified long before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd focus on getting good at the job, fewer mistakes, more categories, and ask Hassan about the pay band. I'd save the extra money instead of spending it. And I'd plan to start the course in two or three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Still a little worried about money, but that's normal for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'm not someone who waits forever, I just like to see others go first. When Dina's sure the pharmacy work is steady, I'll follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a pay rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save half and send a bit more to Mum. And a new mattress, honestly, mine's awful.

I'd tell anxious friends to **plan** and get qualified.
think: I could stay in buying for a while and reach the **pay band** first.
I'd be **qualified** long before 2036 without rushing.
do: Get better at the job and ask Hassan about the **pay band**.
**Save** any extra money instead of spending it.
Plan to start the **technician course** in two or three years.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with the usual small **money** worry.
S4.quote: I'm not someone who waits forever, I just like to see others go first.
fieldNote: With ten years Yara's job worry eases to **background unease**.
She follows **proven paths**, using her friend Dina as a signal.
Even a pay rise goes first to **savings and family**.

steps.text: Ask Hassan about reaching the buyer pay band

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd need time I don't have and money I don't have. What would help is part-time courses that are free for people already working, and some help with rent while you train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people we send money to. If I lose my job, my mum loses something too. It's never just one person.

headlineQuote: If I lose my job, my mum loses something too. It's never just one person.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old** junior buyer of baby care and first aid lines at a pharmacy wholesaler.
She lives alone on **one income**, sends money to her mum, and has about **two weeks** of savings.
She uses AI **sometimes** and prefers to follow paths others have proven.
Her plan in every fast picture is a part-time **pharmacy technician** course, timed against the robot gap.
She stays outwardly **practical** while privately counting how long she'd last.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she lacks both the time and money to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Free part-time courses** for working people and help with **rent** while training.
